editorialFraming: Thirty venues across the Mornington Peninsula that defined the year. Cross-category, ranked, editor-selected. The cuts are hard by design — the point of thirty is that thirty has to mean something. Updated annually each May.
editorsLetter: The Insider's 30 is the Peninsula Insider editorial desk's annual answer to a single question: if you could only point a friend at thirty places on the Mornington Peninsula in a year, which thirty? It sits across categories deliberately. A Walk of the Year that rivals the Restaurant of the Year is the Peninsula's whole proposition. Selections are editorial — visited, verified, and cross-checked against the year's reader feedback. There is no paid placement, ever. The list updates the first weekend of May each year and stays current at /insiders-30/ until then.

picks.blurb: The single dining room that justified the most weekend drives in 2026. Fire-led, regionally rooted, and confident enough to keep the menu tight.
The cellar door + dining room hybrid the rest of the ridge measures itself against. A masterclass in pacing.
The long-lunch room that scales without losing the plot. The grounds, the Piazza, the tasting bar — every door is a different right answer.
Sculpture park, hatted dining, casual deck — the Peninsula's most layered single property.
Architectural confidence the rest of the region rarely matches. Worth the splurge for the right occasion.
Two-hatted, ridge-quiet, and cooking with the conviction of a kitchen that has nothing to prove.
The Pt Leo Estate fine-dining room that earns the price with technique and produce in equal measure.
Red Hill cellar door + restaurant whose pinot is the benchmark and whose room is the unfussiest serious dining on the ridge.
The estate that taught the Peninsula how to do long lunches well. Still does.
Walk-in, hand-poured, no-bookings energy — the Peninsula at its most conversational.
The thermal complex that found its architectural confidence and built the day around the soak.
The category's senior — sprawling, ritual-led, and still a singular Peninsula day out.
The bay-side classic that re-earned its place this year through quiet rooms and a kitchen with new edges.
The Sorrento heritage stay that came back. Bones, light, and the right kind of restraint.
The pub-with-rooms model done right. A counter meal and a window seat is the entire Peninsula in one.
Distillery whose gin botanical walks and tasting flights doubled as a Peninsula geography lesson.
Small-producer cellar door that's quietly become the Saturday afternoon people compare other Saturday afternoons to.
Jackalope's signature room where the design and the menu finally converged in 2026. Worth the ride to the bottom of the ridge.
Lakeside winery dining that punches above its postcode and stays bookable on a normal Saturday.
Rare Hare's casual energy plus a cellar door doing the work — the Peninsula's quiet all-rounder.
The cellar door whose chardonnay is the regional benchmark and whose tasting room is the most thoughtful in Merricks.
Single-block expressions of pinot and chardonnay; a tasting that makes the rest of the day taste different.
The Peninsula's foundational pinot grower; appointment-only, family-run, and unimpeachable.
The all-weather Red Hill anchor whose deck is the photograph everyone's family shared in 2026.
The Mornington roaster + café whose breakfast plates have stayed honest as the rest of the bay polished up.
The mid-Peninsula bakery doing the small-town work the cellar doors quietly depend on.
A bakery, but in the way that defines whether a village has gravity. Flinders does.
A producer-as-day-out that the cellar-door circuit folds around. The cheese alone justifies the loop.
Family-grade A; pick-your-own that doubles as the children's most-shared Peninsula memory of the year.
The 36-hole resort whose course conditioning and staff attention put it in serious-golf-trip territory.
